title: The guru
hook: Hindu paths give the teacher a weighty place, a relationship to approach with care

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's question: who am I, followed rather than answered. Your line was who am I. When a strong thought grabbed you, did you ask to whom it came? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-eight.

Who taught you to tie your shoes? Not a manual. Somebody knelt down, took the laces, went slowly, and let you get it wrong a few times. Some things travel well in books. Some, it seems, only travel hand to hand, from a person who can do them to a person who wants to. In the Upanishads, this kind of teaching is pictured that way: not downloaded, but handed on, by someone who has walked the road, to someone just starting out. That person has a name, and it has become an English word, worn thin by headlines about marketing and fitness. Today's word is the original: guru.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU TO TIE YOUR SHOES?` → `HAND TO HAND, NOT BY MANUAL.` → `A WORD WORN THIN.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit, guru is a teacher, and as an ordinary adjective it also means heavy, weighty. A guru is someone whose words carry weight. There's a traditional explanation too, found in a later text, that hears the syllables as darkness and its remover. It's a teaching, more than a dictionary entry, but it shows how the role is felt. The Mundaka Upanishad gives the scene. A seeker who wants to know what is real should go to a teacher with fuel in hand, a small gift for the teacher's fire. And it names what to look for: a teacher learned in the sacred texts, and established in Brahman, the ultimate reality. Two tests, not one. Knowing the texts isn't enough. Living what they point to isn't either. Both. The Bhagavad Gita adds the student's side. Learn it, Krishna tells Arjuna, by bowing, by asking questions, and by service; the wise who have seen the truth will teach you. Asking questions is right there in the verse. The student isn't asked to stop thinking. And the same texts that honor the teacher also warn. The Katha Upanishad describes people wise in their own eyes, going round and round, like the blind led by the blind. That's why this relationship asks for care. A guru is trusted with a great deal: a student's time, attention, hopes, sometimes a whole life. Trust that weighty is the point of the relationship, and it's exactly why it should be given slowly, with eyes open, and with both of the Mundaka's tests in mind. Yesterday's teacher, Ramana, was such a figure for the people who came to his hill. The question was his gift. The weight of the role is today's lesson.
screen: `GURU: WEIGHTY, A TEACHER.` · `FUEL IN HAND, TO ONE WHO KNOWS AND LIVES IT.` · `BOW, ASK, SERVE.` · `THE BLIND LED BY THE BLIND.` · then, large: `TRUST THAT WEIGHTY, GIVEN SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about what you'd want in a teacher. Settle, and breathe. First, bring to mind one person who taught you something that mattered, in school, at work, on a path. What made their teaching land? Then picture a teacher for the deepest things you care about. Name three qualities you'd look for. Now set them beside the Mundaka's two: do they know the tradition, and do they live it? And one more, from the Gita: would they welcome your questions? The bell holds the time.
Guru. In Sanskrit, a teacher, and weighty: someone whose words carry weight, trusted to hand on what books can't. Today's word.

Your line: choose with care. Today, before you take someone's advice on something that matters, a podcast, a coach, a feed, ask the two questions: do they know it, and do they live it? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: In Hindu traditions that center on a guru, a student seeks out a teacher, often receives instruction or a mantra from them, learns through questions and service, and honors teachers on festivals such as Guru Purnima.

myth: guru only ever meant remover of darkness
as an ordinary adjective it means heavy, weighty. the darkness-remover explanation is a traditional teaching found in a later text.
in the Gita, the student learns by asking questions as well as by service
bowing, asking questions and service: questions are right there in the verse.
the Mundaka asks only that the teacher know the texts
two tests: learned in the sacred texts, and established in Brahman.

fork.setup: you meet a teacher who is brilliant on stage, but you can't tell whether they live what they teach. by the Mundaka's test, what now?
options: follow them: look how moved everyone is.
look for both: learning, and a life rooted in what's taught.
fork.reveal: the Mundaka names two qualities, learned in the texts and established in Brahman. the texts honor the teacher and still ask for care.

original.note: Sanskrit: teacher; as an adjective, heavy, weighty.

trapdoor: what you thought: a guru is any expert, like a marketing guru.
what it means: a spiritual teacher in Hindu paths, trusted with a great deal, and so to be chosen with care.
what a scholar hears: guru, weighty. Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.12 sends the seeker, fuel in hand, to a teacher learned and established in Brahman; Katha 1.2.5 warns of the blind led by the blind.

notes: 'Guru' as adjective 'heavy, weighty' is a standard dictionary sense (Monier-Williams); confirm it is acceptable under the etymology rule, since it's a meaning, not a derivation.
The gu (darkness) / ru (remover) explanation is attributed to 'a later text' (Advaya Taraka Upanishad 16, as usually cited) and called a teaching, not a dictionary derivation. Confirm verse number.
Mundaka 1.2.12 (samit-pani; shrotriyam brahma-nishtham), Gita 4.34 (pranipatena pariprashnena sevaya) and Katha 1.2.5 (andhenaiva niyamana yathandhah; also in Mundaka 1.2.8) are paraphrased. Confirm.
